Leonhard Euler. A Swiss mathematician and physicist from seventeen hundred seven to seventeen eighty-three whose prolific output—roughly one paper per week for fifty-six years—shaped modern mathematics more broadly than perhaps any single figure in history. He formalised the notation we still use: the letter e for the exponential base, i for the imaginary unit, f of x for functions, and the summation symbol sigma. He founded graph theory, advanced the study of analysis and complex numbers, and wrote authoritatively across mechanics, astronomy, and philosophy. Most remarkably, even after going blind late in life—he lost vision in one eye early and then went completely blind—his productivity never ceased. He dictated papers to assistants until his death.

Euler defined the exponential function e to the x rigorously and recognised e, approximately two point seven one eight two eight, as a fundamental constant, the base of natural logarithms. This number appears throughout mathematics and nature with remarkable frequency. His most famous discovery is Euler's formula: e to the i x equals cosine of x plus i times sine of x. This breathtaking equation bridges exponentials, trigonometry, and complex numbers in a single expression, revealing a profound unity in mathematics. The Euler-Lagrange equations form the cornerstone of variational calculus and underpin the Lagrangian formulation of mechanics.

In graph theory, he solved the famous Seven Bridges of Königsberg problem by abstracting it as a graph—paths and nodes instead of bridges and islands—and in doing so, he founded modern graph theory. The Euler characteristic, expressed as V minus E plus F equals two for polyhedra, relates vertices, edges, and faces, and generalises to topological spaces. He also advanced combinatorics and the study of partitions.

He rigorously studied complex numbers, treating them as a field with algebraic properties, and made important discoveries in prime numbers and infinite series. Throughout his life, which was marked by personal tragedy like bankruptcy and loss of sight, and geopolitical upheaval during the Napoleonic era, his curiosity never dimmed. His papers—many unpublished at his death—kept scholars busy for decades afterward. Modern mathematics still inherits his notation, his conceptual frameworks, and his willingness to push algebra and calculus into new and unexplored territories. For students and researchers, Euler remains a model of fearless intellectual exploration.
